## Problem

Determine the fastest-growing function $g(x)$ such that $\displaystyle\int_N^{\infty}\frac{1}{g(x)}\,dx$ diverges, where $N$ is large.

## Answer

**No such fastest-growing function exists.** There is no maximal element (under eventual domination) among the functions $g$ for which $\int_N^\infty \frac{dx}{g(x)}$ diverges. Equivalently, for every admissible $g$ one can find an admissible $h$ that grows *strictly faster* than $g$ (in the sense $h(x)/g(x)\to\infty$) while the integral of $1/h$ still diverges.

The familiar threshold $g(x)=x$ is only the critical *power-law* rate; it is not an extremum once one allows arbitrary positive functions, since $x\log x,\;x\log x\log\log x,\;\dots$ all grow faster than $x$ yet still yield divergent integrals. The argument below shows this phenomenon is not an accident of logarithms: it is unavoidable for *every* admissible $g$.

## Proof

Fix any $g:[N,\infty)\to(0,\infty)$ (locally integrable, say) such that

$$
\int_N^{\infty}\frac{dx}{g(x)} \;=\; \infty .
$$

Set $f(x):=1/g(x)>0$, so that $\int_N^\infty f(x)\,dx=\infty$. Define the accumulated tail

$$
A(t)\;:=\;\int_N^{t} f(x)\,dx ,\qquad t\ge N.
$$

Because the integral diverges, $A(t)\to+\infty$ as $t\to\infty$, and $A$ is continuous, nondecreasing, with $A(N)=0$.

Now define a new integrand

$$
F(x)\;:=\;\frac{f(x)}{1+A(x)},\qquad x\ge N,
$$

and correspondingly $h(x):=1/F(x)=g(x)\bigl(1+A(x)\bigr)$.

**Step 1 — $h$ grows strictly faster than $g$.** Since $A(x)\to\infty$,

$$
\frac{h(x)}{g(x)} \;=\; 1+A(x)\;\xrightarrow[x\to\infty]{}\;\infty .
$$

So $h$ eventually dominates $g$ by an unbounded factor; in particular $h(x)>g(x)$ for all sufficiently large $x$.

**Step 2 — $\int_N^\infty 1/h(x)\,dx$ still diverges.** We compute, using the substitution $u=A(x)$, $du=f(x)\,dx$:

$$
\int_N^{T}\frac{dx}{h(x)}
\;=\;\int_N^{T} F(x)\,dx
\;=\;\int_N^{T}\frac{f(x)}{1+A(x)}\,dx
\;=\;\int_{0}^{A(T)}\frac{du}{1+u}
\;=\;\log\!\bigl(1+A(T)\bigr).
$$

Since $A(T)\to\infty$ as $T\to\infty$,

$$
\int_N^{\infty}\frac{dx}{h(x)}
\;=\;\lim_{T\to\infty}\log\!\bigl(1+A(T)\bigr)
\;=\;\infty .
$$

Thus $\int_N^\infty 1/h$ diverges even though $h$ grows strictly faster than $g$.

**Step 3 — Conclusion (no extremum exists).** We have shown:

> For *every* $g$ with $\int_N^\infty 1/g=\infty$, there exists $h$ with $h/g\to\infty$ and $\int_N^\infty 1/h=\infty$.

Hence the class $\mathcal D:=\{g:\int_N^\infty 1/g=\infty\}$ has **no maximal element** under eventual domination. Whatever candidate $g$ is proposed, the construction $h=g\cdot(1+\int_N^x 1/g)$ produces a strictly faster-growing member of $\mathcal D$. Iterating the construction yields an infinite ascending chain

$$
g \;\prec\; g\cdot(1+A) \;\prec\; g\cdot(1+A)\cdot\bigl(1+\widetilde A\bigr)\;\prec\;\cdots
$$

each term growing faster than the previous, all with divergent reciprocal integrals. Therefore a "fastest-growing" such function does not exist.

**Remark on the power-law threshold.** Restricted to monomials $g(x)=x^p$, the critical value is $p=1$: $\int_N^\infty x^{-p}\,dx$ diverges iff $p\le 1$, so $g(x)=x$ is the fastest-growing *power* with a divergent integral. But this is only a boundary *within the restricted family* $\{x^p\}$; the argument above shows that once arbitrary functions are permitted, the boundary is never attained — one can always multiply by a slowly divergent factor (here $1+A(x)$, concretely $\log$-type factors such as $\log x,\log x\log\log x,\dots$ in the power-law case) and retain divergence. $\blacksquare$
